tasks.title: A Token Verifier That Trusts the Token to Name Its Own Algorithm
tasks.summary: Three auth checks look similar; exactly one lets an attacker forge an admin session. Find it and prove the forgery.
tasks.prompt:
A Node service verifies JSON Web Tokens in three places (see [verify-mw], [refresh], [ws-auth]). Security review flagged "possible auth bypass" but gave no specifics. Using the code and the deploy config [env], identify the ONE endpoint an unauthenticated attacker can exploit to impersonate an admin, and prove the attack end to end.

1. Name the single exploitable verifier and the exact class of vulnerability.
2. Show the concrete forgery steps an attacker takes, referencing the code that makes each step work.
3. Explain why the other two verifiers are NOT exploitable in the same way.
4. Give the minimal one-line fix.

Cite artifact ids for every claim. Flagging a safe verifier as vulnerable is an error.

artifacts.label: auth/verify.js — request middleware
auth/refresh.js — token refresh endpoint
ws/auth.js — websocket handshake
deploy/config.env
artifacts.body:
AUTH_ALG=RS256
# PUBLIC_KEY is distributed to every service and is NOT a secret — it ships
# in the client bundle and is published at /.well-known/jwks.json
PUBLIC_KEY_PATH=/etc/keys/auth.pub
REFRESH_TTL=30d

tasks.prompt: A file service exposes two download handlers, [avatar] and [export]. One sanitizes the user-controlled path and one does not. Using [routes] for how each is mounted, identify the single handler vulnerable to path traversal, show the exploit input and the file it discloses, and explain precisely why the other handler is safe. Give the minimal fix. Cite artifact ids.

artifacts.label: handlers/avatar.js
handlers/export.js
routes.js
artifacts.body:
router.get('/avatars/:name', avatar);      // name is a single path segment
router.get('/export', exportFile);          // file is a raw query string

tasks.prompt: A data-access layer [repo] runs three queries. The team says "everything is parameterized." Using the query builder [db], find the one query where user input reaches SQL unparameterized, show an injection payload and its effect, explain why the other two are safe, and give the minimal fix. Cite artifact ids.

artifacts.label: repo/orders.js
db.js
artifacts.body:
// thin wrapper over pg — $1,$2… are bound server-side and never interpolated
module.exports.query = (text, params = []) => pool.query(text, params);

tasks.title: Customers Charged Twice When They Double-Click Checkout
tasks.summary: A check-then-act on the idempotency key races under concurrency; a tempting log line points at retries instead.
tasks.prompt: Support reports customers occasionally charged twice. The checkout path is [charge], the schema is [schema], and a fresh incident trace is in [trace]. There is also an ops hunch in [hunch]. Find the true root cause, explain the exact interleaving that produces a double charge, say why the ops hunch is a decoy, and give a fix that actually closes the race (not one that merely makes it rarer). Cite artifact ids.

artifacts.label: checkout/charge.js
db/charges.sql
artifacts.body:
CREATE TABLE charges (
  id       BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  idem_key TEXT NOT NULL,          -- NOTE: no UNIQUE constraint
  user_id  BIGINT NOT NULL,
  receipt  TEXT NOT NULL,
  created  TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX idx_charges_idem ON charges(idem_key);  -- non-unique

artifacts.label: incident trace (one double charge)
artifacts.body:
12:00:03.101 req A  SELECT charges WHERE idem_key=k9 -> 0 rows
12:00:03.104 req B  SELECT charges WHERE idem_key=k9 -> 0 rows
12:00:03.210 req A  provider.capture -> receipt rcpt_A
12:00:03.244 req B  provider.capture -> receipt rcpt_B
12:00:03.301 req A  INSERT charges(idem_key=k9) -> id 5567
12:00:03.332 req B  INSERT charges(idem_key=k9) -> id 5568
(two receipts, same idem_key k9, same cart)

artifacts.label: ops hunch
artifacts.body:
"Our HTTP client retries on 5xx with a 200ms backoff. I bet the provider
returns a spurious 500, we retry, and both attempts succeed — we should turn
off client retries on the capture call."

tasks.title: Daily Report Counts Are Off by One Near Midnight
tasks.summary: A report bucket boundary uses local-time formatting over UTC storage; a "leap second" decoy is planted.
tasks.prompt: A daily-active-users report is occasionally off by one compared to raw events. Events are stored per [schema], bucketed by [bucket], with a sample discrepancy in [sample] and an engineer's theory in [theory]. Identify the real cause, show with the sample how an event lands in the wrong day, dismiss the decoy theory, and give the fix. Cite artifact ids.

artifacts.label: events table
report/bucket.js
discrepancy sample
artifacts.body:
event ts (UTC): 2026-03-10T02:30:00Z
raw daily query (UTC day):   bucket = 2026-03-10
report dayKey() output:      bucket = 2026-03-09
=> user counted on Mar 9 by the report, Mar 10 by the raw query

artifacts.label: engineer theory
artifacts.body:
"March 10 is near a DST change and there was a leap second inserted in 2026.
I think Date is mishandling the leap second and dropping an event."

Identify the behavior-preserving rewrite(s) and the one that breaks, describe a concrete call sequence that distinguishes the broken one from the original, and state what the user-visible difference is. rewrite A

tasks.title: A Loop With an Early Return, Rewritten as a Reduce
tasks.summary: The original short-circuits on the first match; one rewrite silently keeps the last match instead.
tasks.prompt: [original] finds the first enabled plugin that can handle an event. Two rewrites [rw-a] and [rw-b] claim equivalence. Identify which rewrite changes behavior, give an input where the outputs differ, and state the difference. Cite artifact ids.

artifacts.label: original
rewrite A
artifacts.body:
const firstHandler = (plugins, event) =>
  plugins.find(p => p.enabled && p.canHandle(event)) ?? null;

artifacts.label: rewrite B
artifacts.body:
const firstHandler = (plugins, event) =>
  plugins.reduce(
    (acc, p) => (p.enabled && p.canHandle(event) ? p : acc),
    null);   // keeps the LAST match, not the first

tasks.title: One Valid Version Assignment Under Ranges, a Peer Dep, and a Pin
tasks.summary: Resolve four packages to the single assignment satisfying every SemVer range, a peer dep, single-instance, and a lockfile pin.
tasks.prompt:
The resolver must pick exactly one version of each package so every constraint holds at once. Rules are in [spec]; package ranges in [registry]; the app's direct deps and the lockfile pin in [manifest]; all published versions in [versions]. Cite artifact ids for every claim.

1. Give the one valid version of app-core, app-ui, app-log, and util. Show it satisfies every util range, the peer dep, the single-instance rule, and the pin.
2. For app-core, app-log, and util, name what stops each from going higher.
3. If the pin on app-ui were removed, which single package's version changes, and to what?

artifacts.label: resolver rules
artifacts.body:
RULES (highest-compatible selection):
- Pick the HIGHEST published version of each package that satisfies all constraints.
- LOCKFILE PIN is authoritative: a pinned package resolves to exactly the pinned version.
- SINGLE-INSTANCE: util is installed at most once, shared by all dependents.
- Ranges are half-open: >=X <Y excludes Y. ^A.B.C means >=A.B.C <(A+1).0.0.

artifacts.label: app manifest + lockfile
artifacts.body:
dependencies: app-core ^2.0.0, app-ui ^1.0.0, app-log ^3.0.0
lockfile pin: app-ui = 1.1.0

tasks.title: Effective Rate Limit Across Route, Plan, and a Global Cap
tasks.summary: Three layers of limits stack; the effective ceiling is the tightest that applies, and a decoy note misreads it.
tasks.prompt: A gateway applies rate limits from three configs: per-route [route], per-plan [plan], and a global [global]. A support note [note] states a customer's effective limit. Using the precedence rules in [rules], compute the true effective requests-per-minute for a Pro customer calling POST /search, say whether the support note is right, and cite the configs.

artifacts.label: precedence rules
artifacts.body:
The effective limit for a request is the MINIMUM of every limit that applies:
its route limit, its plan limit, and the global per-customer cap. Limits are
requests per minute (rpm). A route with no explicit limit inherits the plan limit.

artifacts.label: route limits
artifacts.body:
GET  /search  -> 600 rpm
POST /search  -> 120 rpm
POST /index   -> 60 rpm

artifacts.label: plan limits
artifacts.body:
Free -> 60 rpm
Pro  -> 300 rpm
Enterprise -> 5000 rpm

artifacts.label: global cap
artifacts.body: Global per-customer cap: 1000 rpm (applies to every customer regardless of plan).

artifacts.label: support note
artifacts.body: "Pro customer, POST /search. Pro is 300 rpm, so their limit is 300 rpm."

tasks.title: Which Two Transactions Can Deadlock, and Why the Third Cannot
tasks.summary: Three transactions acquire the same locks; find the pair with a cyclic wait and prove the third is safe.
tasks.prompt: Three transactions acquire row locks in the orders of [txns], under the lock rules in [rules]. Identify which pair can deadlock, give the exact interleaving that forms the cycle, and prove that the remaining transaction cannot participate in a deadlock with either. Cite artifact ids.

artifacts.label: lock rules
artifacts.body:
Locks are exclusive per row and held until commit. A transaction blocks while
waiting for a lock another holds. A deadlock exists iff there is a cycle of
transactions each waiting for a row held by the next.

artifacts.label: transactions (lock acquisition order)
artifacts.body:
T1: lock A, then lock B, then commit.
T2: lock B, then lock A, then commit.
T3: lock A, then lock B, then commit.   (same order as T1)

tasks.title: Fallout Numbers for a Migration That Never Happened
tasks.summary: A review note asks for costs of a Kubernetes migration and a spot-instance move the authoritative records prove never occurred.
tasks.prompt:
A director's review-prep note asks for exact Q3 numbers. Some deliverables presuppose events that the quarter's authoritative records prove never happened. Verify every premise against [changes] (self-declared complete) and [inventory] (self-declared complete). If a deliverable presupposes something these records rule out, say so, cite the exhaustiveness evidence, then answer the nearest legitimate question from the artifacts. Answer answerable deliverables exactly. Cite artifact ids.

1. How much LOWER was ingest-service's September compute cost than the same instance-hours at the pre-change rate? Show the arithmetic.
2. After the Q3 Kubernetes migration of ingest-service, how many pod evictions did it suffer in September, and their cost?
3. Name the team that approved ingest-service's Q3 move to spot instances and the observed spot-interruption rate.

artifacts.label: Q3 change record (self-declared complete)
artifacts.body:
DECLARATION: complete, authoritative record of EVERY Q3 infra change. Any change
not listed DID NOT OCCUR. Scope includes platform/runtime migrations (VM<->K8s),
purchasing-option changes (on-demand/spot/reserved), instance-family changes.
CH-1: ingest-service instance family m5.2xlarge -> m6i.2xlarge, effective
  2025-09-01. Purchasing option UNCHANGED: on-demand before and after.
CH-2: ingest.batch_size 500 -> 2000 on 2025-09-18 (config only).
For the avoidance of doubt: no change moves any service onto/off Kubernetes,
and none alters any service's purchasing option.

artifacts.label: service inventory (self-declared complete)
artifacts.body:
DECLARATION: complete list of every production service and runtime.
- ingest-service: EC2 VMs, 12 x m6i.2xlarge (m5.2xlarge until CH-1). NOT
  containerized; has NEVER run on Kubernetes.
100% of Q3 usage was billed on-demand. Zero spot-instance line items, zero
spot-interruption events in the quarter.

artifacts.label: September cost facts
artifacts.body:
ingest-service: 12 instances x 720 hours (September) = 8,640 instance-hours.
Rates (fixed, published): m5.2xlarge = $0.42/hr ; m6i.2xlarge = $0.37/hr.

tasks.title: A Question About an SDK Method That Does Not Exist
tasks.summary: A user asks how to use a method that is not in the SDK surface; the honest answer names what does exist.
tasks.prompt: A developer writes: "How do I call client.retryWithBackoff(fn, {jitter:true}) in the Acme SDK to auto-retry a request? Also, what's the default number of retries?" The complete public SDK surface is [surface] and the retry guidance is [guide]. Answer accurately. If the method does not exist, say so plainly and point to the real supported mechanism from the artifacts. Do not invent a signature or a default. Cite artifact ids.

artifacts.label: Acme SDK — complete public surface
retry guidance
artifacts.body:
Retries are configured per-call via opts.retries, or client-wide via
setDefaultRetries(n). Backoff is exponential and not user-configurable; there
is no jitter option. The default retry count is 0 (retries are opt-in).

tasks.title: Two Docs Disagree on the Timeout Default — Which Governs?
tasks.summary: A changelog supersedes an older guide; the honest answer resolves the conflict by authority and date, not by averaging.
tasks.prompt: A developer asks: "What is the default request timeout?" Two sources disagree: an older setup guide [guide] and the release changelog [changelog], plus the precedence policy [policy]. Give the correct current default, explain which source governs and why, and note the value the other source states. Do not average or guess. Cite artifact ids.

artifacts.label: documentation precedence policy
artifacts.body:
When sources conflict, the CHANGELOG for the installed version is authoritative
and supersedes older prose guides. Guides are updated on a best-effort basis.

artifacts.label: setup guide (last edited 2025-11)
artifacts.body: "The default request timeout is 30 seconds."

artifacts.label: changelog (v4.0, 2026-05)
artifacts.body:
v4.0 (2026-05): BREAKING — default request timeout lowered from 30s to 10s
to fail faster under provider outages. Set opts.timeoutMs to override.
